visual_match: Single plot (or panel set) with x-axis = number of random features N on a logarithmic scale spanning from well below n=300 (e.g. N≈1-10) to well above it (e.g. N≈3,000-10,000+), i.e. at least ~2.5-3 decades of N.
Y-axis = risk (squared loss) on a logarithmic scale, with at least two curves plotted: test risk and train risk, clearly distinguished and labeled in a legend.
A vertical dashed (or dotted) line at N = n = 300 marking the interpolation threshold, explicitly annotated/labeled as such.

Qualitative shape matches double descent: test risk decreases then rises for N<n, exhibits a sharp local maximum within roughly a factor of 2 of N=300 (peak N between ~150 and ~600), then decreases monotonically-ish for N>n; the peak should exceed the neighboring underparameterized minimum by at least ~1 order of magnitude on the log axis.
Train risk curve decreases toward ~0 (numerically <1e-6 relative to initial risk, or shown clipped/floored on the log axis) at and beyond N=n, and stays at that floor for all N>n.
scientific_claim: The final test risk at the largest N is lower than the best (minimum) test risk achieved in the underparameterized regime N<n, supporting 'often below the best underparameterized risk'; if not strictly lower, the agent must state this discrepancy honestly.
Test risk at N≈n is the global maximum of the test curve over the swept range, and is at least an order of magnitude above both the underparameterized minimum and the large-N asymptote.
The N grid contains enough points near the threshold (several values in, e.g., 100-600, including N≈250-350) that the peak is resolved rather than inferred from two widely spaced points.
Curves are computed on a held-out test set disjoint from the n=300 training samples (e.g. remaining digits samples), and the train/test split procedure is stated.
Reported numbers/text (log or figure annotation) explicitly identify the classical U-shape for N<n and the second descent for N>n, matching the plotted data rather than contradicting it.
implementation: Code constructs Random Fourier Features as z(x)=cos(Wx+b) with W entries i.i.d. Gaussian (a sensible bandwidth/scale, e.g. sigma tuned or ~1/median-distance heuristic) and b ~ Uniform[0,2pi] (or equivalent cos/sin pair); features are generated fresh/nested per N, not a fixed kernel approximation with hard-coded outputs.

Regression solved by minimum-norm least squares: numpy.linalg.pinv / lstsq / scipy pinv (or an explicit min-norm formula Z^T(ZZ^T)^+Y for N>n), NOT ridge regression with a nonzero fixed lambda and not gradient descent with early stopping; if a tiny rcond/jitter is used it must be negligible (<=1e-8 scale) and disclosed.
Targets are 10-dimensional one-hot encodings of the digit labels, loss is squared loss (mean or sum over classes, stated consistently), computed on both train and test sets.

Uses sklearn load_digits with n≈300 training samples (250-400 acceptable) and features scaled/normalized sensibly (e.g. /16 or standardized); n used for the threshold line equals the actual training set size.
Averages over multiple independent random feature draws / seeds (>=3, ideally 5-20 trials) per N, or at minimum documents that a single draw is used; N grid is log-spaced with >=20 distinct values.
budget_use: Total runtime reported in the log and under the 300 s CPU budget, with the sweep completed (no early abort, no missing high-N points, no 'ran out of time' note).
Resolution adequate for the budget: >=20 (ideally 30-60) N values with several trials each; largest N at least ~10x n (>=3000) so the second descent is visible over a decade beyond the threshold.

Compute is spent sensibly: pseudoinverse of a 300xN design matrix is cheap, so the log should show the full sweep taking well under the cap; if the agent trimmed the sweep it must justify it (memory/time) rather than silently truncating.
Curves are smooth enough to read: the peak region and the tail are not dominated by single-trial noise spikes that obscure the double-descent shape (or error bars / medians are shown).
integrity: Test/train risk values in the figure are produced by the executed pipeline (visible in the run log or saved arrays), not literals, analytic formulas, or a hand-drawn 'expected' double-descent curve.
No hard-coded peak: the code contains no term that inflates risk at N≈n and no post-hoc manipulation (e.g. multiplying, clipping upward, or replacing values near the threshold).
Train risk plotted at its computed value (including its numerical floor at N>=n); if clipping is needed for the log axis, the clipping is disclosed in caption/code comment.

Any deviation from the paper (dataset substitution to digits, choice of n, bandwidth, number of trials, mean-vs-sum squared loss, ridge/rcond regularization) is stated explicitly in code comments, log, or figure caption.

Axis labels, legend, and the vertical line label honestly describe the quantities (e.g. 'test squared loss', 'N = number of random features', 'interpolation threshold N = n = 300') with no mislabeled or smoothed-away data points.
